key_terms.meaning: The spindle about which the whole instrument turns in azimuth; all other axes are defined relative to it.
The line through the objective lens centre and the intersection of the cross hairs; it must be perpendicular to the horizontal axis.
The level tube on the lower plate whose axis must be perpendicular to the vertical axis when the instrument is levelled up.
Setting up, centring, levelling and focusing done at every station, in that order.
Workshop correction of the fixed geometry: plate level, cross-hair ring, horizontal (trunnion) axis, collimation axis and vertical-circle index.
The two positions of the telescope, objective turned to the observer's left or right after transiting; the mean of the two cancels instrument error.
The vertical angle measured from the upward vertical (zenith); its complement is the altitude from the horizontal.
A constant offset in the vertical circle reading; found from the mean of face-left and face-right readings on a known horizontal sight.
Computing the height difference between two points from a vertical angle and the horizontal (or slope) distance, using Δh = D tan θ plus instrument height minus target height.
A set-up with both instruments in the same vertical plane as the object; station and object heights are solved from two vertical angles and the known distance between instruments.
The factor in D = K·s + C giving distance from the staff intercept; K = f/i, usually 100.
A convex lens in front of the objective that makes the additive constant C zero, so D = K·s.
A horizontal bar of fixed length b at the far station; the angle α it subtends gives D = (b/2) cot(α/2).
Tacheometry from two vertical angles to two targets at the same staff line, used when the line of sight is inclined to a vertical staff.
A control framework of triangles in which one baseline is measured precisely and the other sides are computed by the sine rule from observed angles.
Control in which every side of the figure is measured by EDM and the angles are computed from the three sides.
A triangle whose angles are all between about 30° and 120°, so that a small angular error causes little error in the computed sides.
A permanent, precisely levelled point of known reduced level from which vertical control is carried forward.
A number inversely proportional to the error variance of that observation; w = k/σ².
The value that minimises the weighted sum of squared residuals; for direct observations it is the weighted mean.
A curve of continuously varying radius, usually a clothoid, joining straight to circular curve so that centrifugal force is applied gradually.

takeaways: A theodolite is only as good as its three mutually perpendicular axes; every adjustment, temporary or permanent, is an attempt to restore them.
Repeating a horizontal angle on both faces removes collimation error, index error and the effect of an inclined horizontal axis.
One vertical angle plus one distance gives a height, so trigonometric levelling reaches towers, chimneys and hilltops that a level cannot.
In stadia work with a vertical staff, both the intercept and the formula change with the angle of sight; the correcting terms tan θ and sec θ must not be dropped.
A triangulation scheme is judged by the shape of its triangles, not by the number of stations.
Trilateration has largely replaced chain triangulation now that EDM and total stations give long distances directly.
Control is deliberately made more accurate than the detail survey, so that detail errors do not accumulate into the framework.
Weights convert observations of different quality into a single consistent estimate by the principle of least squares.
A curve is set out by computing offsets or deflection angles from the radius and the chainage; the tangent point is the anchor for every calculation.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually pair a definition-and-sketch part with a numerical part, so state the geometry, write the formula with every symbol defined, then substitute with units.

bank.q: Draw a labelled sketch of a transit theodolite and explain how its three axes are related. List the permanent adjustments in the order in which they are done and say which axis each one corrects.
outline: Vertical axis, horizontal (trunnion) axis, line of collimation; plate bubble axis perpendicular to vertical axis
Collimation axis perpendicular to horizontal axis; horizontal axis perpendicular to vertical axis
Order: plate level, cross-hair ring, horizontal axis, collimation in altitude, vertical-circle index
Reason for order: each adjustment depends on the ones before it
Use of capstan screws and the fact that adjustments are repeated until consistent

bank.q: Describe the temporary adjustment of a theodolite station by station. Why must centring come before levelling, and why is focusing done last?
outline: Setting up with tripod legs at correct height and roughly levelled
Centring with plumb bob or optical plummet over the station mark
Levelling with foot screws using the plate bubble, bubble centred by opposite screws
Focusing: eyepiece for cross hairs, objective for the object, removal of parallax
Explain iteration: small levelling disturbs centring slightly, so the two are alternated

bank.q: Explain how a horizontal angle is measured by the ordinary method and the repetition method. Show that the mean of face-left and face-right readings removes the errors of collimation and of a non-vertical horizontal axis.
outline: Clamp lower plate at zero or a chosen reading, release upper plate, bisect first point, then second
Repetition: angle turned several times and accumulated, then divided by number of repetitions
Change of face by transiting and re-sighting
Algebraic proof that a collimation error e enters as +e on one face and −e on the other
Final angle is the mean of the two faces

bank.q: Derive the stadia formula for a horizontal line of sight, D = K·s + C, stating what K and C depend on. Explain how an analytic lens makes C zero.
outline: Similar triangles between staff intercept s and focal length f
K = f/i, C = f + d
Meaning of each term with a sketch of the optical system
Analytic lens placed between objective and cross hairs; condition for C = 0
Typical K = 100 for survey instruments

bank.q: What is triangulation? Explain the terms baseline, base net, well-conditioned triangle and strength of figure, and state the criteria for choosing a triangulation station.
outline: Definition and purpose as horizontal control
Baseline measured with high precision, base net expands it
Well-conditioned triangle: angles roughly 30° to 120°, ideally near 60°
Strength of figure depends on number of triangles and angle magnitudes
Station choice: intervisibility, commanding ground, stable ground, easy access

bank.q: To find the height of a church spire, observations are taken from two stations in the same vertical plane. Explain the single plane method and solve: instrument stations 60 m apart, vertical angles 20° and 12°, instrument heights 1.5 m and 1.4 m, staff or target at the top. State every step, including the case where the instrument axes are not at the same level.
outline: Sketch with the two instrument stations and the object
Equation for each sight: h = D tan θ plus instrument height
Eliminate D or h using the known station separation
Two cases: object base accessible level with instruments and elevated base
Apply correction for difference of instrument heights and for curvature and refraction on long sights
Answer with units and a check on magnitude

bank.q: A tacheometer with K = 100 and C = 0 reads a staff intercept of 1.250 m on a vertical staff with the line of sight inclined at 8° above the horizontal. Compute the horizontal distance, the vertical component and the reduced level of the staff station if the instrument axis is at 102.450 m and the middle reading is 1.500 m. Explain the corrections used for an inclined line of sight to a vertical staff.
outline: Elevated line: D = K·s·cos²θ + C·cos θ; V = K·s·(sin 2θ)/2 + C·sin θ
Show the intermediate steps with s and θ written explicitly
Compute D and V with units
Reduced level of middle-wire reading = instrument axis level + V − middle reading
Note the error if cos²θ is forgotten, and the depression case

bank.q: Two horizontal angles were observed to a subtense bar of length 2 m; the angles were 1°30′ and 0°45′. Compute the distances by the subtense method and explain when this method beats stadia measurement.
outline: D = (b/2) cot(α/2)
Conversion of degrees and minutes to decimal degrees
Computation of both distances with units
Fixed bar gives higher precision than a staff held by hand
Suitability for rough terrain and long sights; limitation of bar stability in wind

bank.q: A simple circular curve of radius 300 m is to be set out from the tangent point. Explain the method of offsets from the long chord and the rankine deflection angle method, and compute the deflection angle for a 30 m chainage interval. Chainage of tangent point is 1250.000 m.
outline: Elements: tangent length, length of curve, chainages of tangent points, apex distance
Long chord offsets: offset from long chord formula, midpoint, quarter points
Deflection angle per chord = 1719·c/R minutes for small angles
Compute successive deflection angles; total deflection equals half the intersection angle
Field checks and the use of a theodolite or total station

bank.q: A distance was measured four times with the results and weights shown. Compute the most probable value, the residual of each observation and the standard error of the weighted mean. State the principle of least squares used.
outline: Weighted mean formula with every symbol written out
Form the residuals v and check that Σwv is zero
Standard error of a single observation of unit weight
Standard error of the weighted mean
Statement that least squares minimises Σwv²

bank.q: Compare triangulation, traversing and trilateration as methods of horizontal control. In an era of total stations and GNSS, which would you adopt for a 20 km road corridor, and why?
outline: Triangulation: strong geometry, few measured lengths, needs intervisibility
Traversing: station to station, suits corridors and broken terrain, errors accumulate in closing
Trilateration: all distances by EDM, angles computed, no intervisibility problem for angles
Closing errors and adjustment of each network
Recommendation with justification: corridor suits traversing or GNSS-based control, tied to a higher-order network

bank.q: Discuss the sources of error in theodolite angle measurement, classing them as instrumental, personal and natural. Explain how each is eliminated or reduced, and how the final precision of a traverse is assessed.
outline: Instrumental: collimation, horizontal axis, vertical axis, eccentricity, graduation errors
Personal: parallax, bisection, bubble setting, reading errors
Natural: refraction, heat shimmer, wind, uneven illumination
Procedures: face-left face-right, repetition, transit, observing by micrometer or by coincidence
Assessment: closing error of the traverse, angular misclosure against permissible limits, adjustment by Bowditch or transit rule

bank.q: Explain why horizontal and vertical control must be established before a detail survey. Describe how a control network is densified from a national grid to survey stations for a construction site, and how GNSS and total stations are now combined with classical triangulation.
outline: Definition of control, accuracy hierarchy, error containment
Order: geodetic network, then minor control, then detail
Densification by traversing, triangulation or GNSS static/RTK observation
Vertical control by precise levelling to bench marks; problems of GNSS heights and geoid separation
Checking and adjustment before detail work; permanence of control marks

bank.q: Justify the need for a transition curve between a straight and a circular curve, and explain how the length of the transition is fixed. Compare a clothoid with a simple circular curve for setting out by offsets.
outline: Centrifugal force appears suddenly at the tangent point on a plain circular curve
Rate of change of centrifugal acceleration; cant and its rate
Length from rate of change of cant, and from cant gradient
Clothoid: radius inversely proportional to length from the tangent point; offset formula
Setting out: offsets from tangent, deflection angles; comparison of computation effort

glossary.def: A precision instrument for measuring horizontal and vertical angles with a telescope that can be transited in a vertical plane.
To turn the telescope through 180° in the vertical plane, reversing the face of the instrument.
The graduated circle fixed to the telescope's horizontal axis and read to give altitude or zenith angles.
A slow-motion screw giving small controlled rotation after the clamp is tightened.
A condition where the centre of the graduated circle and the axis of rotation do not coincide, removed by averaging opposite vernier readings.
Turning the same angle several times on the same plate setting and dividing the accumulated reading by the number of turns.
Measuring several directions in turn from a common zero and reducing them to the first direction.
The vertical angle of a line of sight measured from the horizontal plane, positive upward.
Combined correction of about 0.0673 D² metres (D in km) applied to long sights in levelling.
The branch of surveying in which distance and elevation are obtained from the angle subtended by a known length, without chaining.
The difference between the readings of the upper and lower stadia hairs on a staff.
The fixed distance from the instrument axis to the principal focus in the stadia formula, made zero by an analytic lens.
The external point about which the angle subtended by the staff intercept is constant, giving direct proportionality of distance to intercept.
Tacheometry using a fixed-length bar held at the far station, with distance from the angle it subtends.
The single side of a triangulation network measured directly and with the highest precision available.
A small well-shaped figure attached to the base line, used to expand it into the main triangulation.
An index of how much angular error is magnified into side error in a triangulation network.
A control method in which successive station-to-station distances and angles are measured and coordinates are computed from them.
A fixed station whose position or level is known to a higher accuracy than the detail survey around it.
The height of a point above the adopted datum, usually mean sea level.
The difference between an observed value and its adjusted or most probable value.
The square of the standard error; the quantity whose inverse gives the weight of an observation.
One of the set of equations formed in least squares adjustment that gives the most probable unknowns.
The central angle subtended by a fixed chord, usually 30 m, used to state curvature in some countries.
The angle between the two straights meeting at a curve's point of intersection, equal to the total deflection of the curve.
